newsitem.title: FRANCE: Digital TV battles in Spain and Germany could end in compromise - Canal Plus.
newsitem.headline: Digital TV battles in Spain and Germany could end in compromise - Canal Plus.

text.p: Battles over whether there will be one or two digital television stations in both Spain and Germany will probably be resolved through a compromise between existing actors leading to just one operator, executives of French pay TV firm Canal Plus said on Thursday.
In Spain, this could be on the cards before the Summer, Pierre Lescure, Canal Plus chairman, told a meeting of analysts on the company's 1996 results.

"I am convinced that between now and the end of the season, that is before the Summer, we could well be approaching a realistic accord which would mean that Spain would have only one programme offering," Lescure said in answer to questions.

This could be done by giving a significant place in the line-up which includes Canalsatellite, Canal Plus's Spanish satellite unit, to Spain's Telefonica, which is currently leading the rival offering, he said.
"It will be necessary to open a broad place to the principal component of the other platform... opposite us, that is obvious. I am thinking of Telefonica," he said.
CanalSatellite is 15 percent owned by commercial channel Antena 3 and 85 percent owned by Sogecable, which is in turn 25 percent owned by Canal Plus and 25 percent owned by Spanish media group Prisa.
The other digital platform is led by the recently privatised telecoms operator Telefonica with participation from the state's Radio and Television of Spain (RTVE) and Mexico's Televisa.
Lescure said Canal Plus's rivals did not even have a decoder yet, while CanalSatellite has signed up 30,000 subscribers and installed 13,000 decoders.
He also said he thought the court case started against Canal Plus in Spain was unlikely to go much further.
"We are particularly unworried about the outcome of the complaint... one cannot imagine this will go very far," he said.
Lescure on Tuesday had a half-hour meeting with the Spanish judge handling the case, over allegations of fraud and misuse of funds against Canal Plus directors.

In Germany, where the development of digital TV has been subject to a clash of media titans, it is unlikely a competitor would emerge to Kirchgruppe's DF1 in digital television, said Marc-Andre Feiffer, a Canal Plus director.
But DF1 will need to talk to a top channel like Canal Plus's Premiere, if it wants to develop, he said.
"It is clear that DF1 cannot develop without access to a premium channel like Premiere," he said in answer to questions.
Beyond the "clash of egos" between the two groups, there was a possibility of compromise, he said.

Australian media magnate Rupert Murdoch's British Sky Broadcasting (BSkyB) earlier this month axed a plan to buy into DF1, which is owned by Bavarian media mogul Leo Kirch, leaving open the possible line-up of forces.

Kirch also has a stake in Premiere, which is currently an analogue channel, but whose partners Canal Plus and Bertelsmann AG are looking to digital television. BSkyB is interested in taking a stake in Premiere, a factor which upset its deal with DF1.

Feiffer said it was also essential that both DF1 and Premiere reached an agreement with Deutsche Telekom, which currently wants them just to deliver programmes on its cable network and leave it the juicier role of dealing with subscribers.
